title: Inverted indexing and posting lists
summary: An inverted index is the structure behind search: for each term, a list of the documents containing it (a postings list), alongside a dictionary of terms. The textbook builds it by collecting documents, tokenizing, normalizing tokens, then indexing, so queries need not scan every text. Being crawled is not being indexed: Google says indexing isn't guaranteed and Search Console reports statuses such as 'Crawled - currently not indexed'. The textbook is a method description, not proof of Google's internals.
actions: Treat 'crawled' and 'indexed' as separate states when auditing; check the Page indexing report status, not just server logs.
Diagnose crawled-but-not-indexed and discovered-but-not-crawled as different problems.
Do not assume a robots.txt Disallow removes a URL from the index; use noindex or password protection.
Do not promise clients that every published page will be indexed.

myths.myth: If Googlebot fetched a page, it is in the index.
myths.correction: Google says indexing isn't guaranteed and defines 'Crawled - currently not indexed' as crawled but not indexed.

myths.myth: The textbook inverted index is exactly how Google stores pages.
myths.correction: Practitioner inference: the quoted textbook passages describe a method, and nothing saved says how any engine is built.

items.prompt: In the textbook's inverted index, the index consists of a dictionary and what?
items.explanation: The textbook says the final step creates an inverted index consisting of a dictionary and postings. A term's list of documents is called a postings list.

items.prompt: Why does the textbook index documents in advance? This describes the textbook, not a specific engine.
options: A. Removes the need to tokenize text
B. Guarantees every crawled page is returned
C. Avoids scanning every text for each query
D. Replaces the dictionary with a single list
items.explanation: Correct: the textbook says indexing in advance is the way to avoid linearly scanning the texts for each query. Tokenizing is still needed (it is step 2 of building the index). Nothing in the textbook says every crawled page is returned; Google says indexing isn't guaranteed. The dictionary is kept alongside postings, not replaced.

items.prompt: True or false: in the textbook's inverted index, postings are secondarily sorted by document ID.
items.explanation: The textbook states: the postings are secondarily sorted by docID.

items.prompt: The textbook says the term-document matrix is 'extremely sparse', meaning it has few entries of what kind? Answer with one word, no hyphen (a form of 'zero').
items.explanation: The textbook says the matrix is extremely sparse, that is, it has few non-zero entries, and presents the inverted index as the central structure that avoids scanning the texts. Practitioner inference: this is why storing only the documents that contain each term is efficient.

items.prompt: True or false: Google says every page it processes will be indexed.
items.explanation: Google says indexing isn't guaranteed; not every page that Google processes will be indexed.

items.prompt: Which statement is NOT supported by the saved sources?
options: A. The textbook calls a term's list of documents a postings list
B. The textbook says the term-document matrix is extremely sparse
C. Google says indexing isn't guaranteed for every processed page
D. Google's index is built exactly as the textbook describes
items.explanation: Correct (unsupported): the textbook describes a method; it is not proof of how Google's index is built. The other three are supported: a term's document list is a postings list, the matrix is extremely sparse, and Google says indexing isn't guaranteed.

items.prompt: Textbook order of building an inverted index: collect documents, tokenize, ___, then index. Fill the blank (two words).
items.explanation: The textbook lists: collect documents, tokenize, do linguistic preprocessing (producing normalized tokens, the indexing terms), then create the index of dictionary and postings.

items.prompt: An audit note set mixes definitions of Search Console indexing statuses. Which note is wrong?
options: A. Crawled - currently not indexed means fetched but not indexed
B. A URL fetched with a 200 by Googlebot is therefore indexed
C. Discovered - currently not indexed means found but not yet crawled
D. Indexing isn't guaranteed for pages Google processes
items.explanation: Correct (the error): Google says crawled and indexed are different: indexing isn't guaranteed, and the 'Crawled' status means crawled but not indexed. The other notes match Google's definitions of the two statuses and its indexing statement.

items.prompt: HYPOTHETICAL blog with 300 new posts. Symptom: none appear in search. Evidence: (1) logs show Googlebot fetched all 300 URLs; (2) robots.txt allows them; (3) Search Console lists them as 'Crawled - currently not indexed'. What does the evidence establish?
options: A. Googlebot has not discovered these URLs yet
B. The robots.txt file is blocking these posts
C. Fetched, not indexed; no guarantee of it
D. The posts need noindex tags before fetching
items.explanation: Correct: Google's definition of that status is crawled but not indexed, and Google says indexing is not guaranteed. So crawl access is not the blocker. Googlebot found the URLs (they were fetched). A robots block would show a different status ('blocked by robots.txt'). noindex tags would keep pages out, not make them fetchable.

items.prompt: HYPOTHETICAL site. Goal: keep /print/ pages out of Google. Evidence: (1) /print/ URLs are disallowed in robots.txt; (2) Search Console shows 'Indexed, though blocked by robots.txt' for some; (3) other sites link to them. Best fix?
options: A. Add more Disallow lines covering the same URLs
B. Use noindex or password protection, not robots.txt alone
C. Add all the print URLs to the XML sitemap
D. Return a 5xx status for the print URLs
items.explanation: Correct: Google says a disallowed page can still be indexed if linked from other sites and that noindex or password protection is how to keep a page out. More Disallow lines repeat the failed approach. A sitemap invites inclusion. A 5xx is not a stated method. Practitioner inference: a noindex tag has to be fetched to be seen, so the URLs likely must be crawlable.
